source.title: ZerO Initialization: Initializing Residual Networks with only Zeros and Ones
source.authors: Jia-Wei Zhao; F. Schäfer; Anima Anandkumar

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares initialization methods on CIFAR-10 ResNets at increasing depths, including without batch normalization, and reports accuracy over 15 epochs. This bears on the tested no-normalization and depth portions of V3 and V6, using accuracy rather than training error.
record.gate_note: Most benchmark tables report test error or test perplexity, not training classification error, so they do not establish near-zero training error. Figure 4 reports test accuracy over 15 epochs for deep CIFAR-10 ResNets; this is the relevant result for V3 and V6. The paper also reports a warmup effect on gradient norms, but that does not test V5's above-stability-limit loss and curvature behavior.
record.test_reason: Figure 4 compares CIFAR-10 ResNets with and without batch normalization after 15 epochs. The authors explicitly report that ZerO without batch normalization matches the batch-normalized baseline, bearing on V6's accuracy-speed claim under a different initialization. It does not establish V3's training-error claims or V4's claims about plain networks.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that deterministic ZerO initialization achieves competitive benchmark performance, enables stable training of very deep ResNets without batch normalization, produces low-rank learning trajectories and sparse solutions, and improves reproducibility. Their depth-experiment text reports matching the batch-normalized baseline; it does not report near-zero training classification error.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes deterministic ZerO initialization and compares it with Fixup, ReZero, and Kaiming initialization; it does not reproduce the claim's cited experiments or measure training classification error.
record.method_sensitivity: For ZerO, learning-rate warmup materially changes early gradient norms; the paper says warmup is essential for using a large maximal learning rate. In the depth comparison, performance varies with network depth and initialization.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard Transformer initialization diverges at 10 and 20 layers; ZerO obtains test perplexities of 145.62 and 141.81.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization changes trainable depth in residual Transformer architectures; V4 specifies plain networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 1 and Figure 3 establish persistent activation-dimension and residual-weight rank constraints under partial identity initialization, which Hadamard initialization can break.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization can constrain expressivity through feature-subspace alignment; rank constraints alone do not measure the training-speed or depth effects named in V4.

fits_no_version.finding: Warmup substantially reduces ZerO's early gradient norms, whereas Kaiming and Xavier gradient norms change little.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: ZerO's early gradient behavior depends on the initial learning rate; this does not establish above-threshold recovery or curvature dynamics in V5.

record.problems: The relevant depth result is presented as a plot without numerical values in the text. It reports test accuracy over 15 epochs rather than training classification error, and does not state uncertainty for this comparison.
record.rows_left_out: No rows retained: the supplied text describes Figure 4's comparison in prose but gives no exact per-method, per-depth values. The figure-only accuracy curves are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text. Other benchmark tables report test error or perplexity, which do not measure the training-error claims.

Learning speed and trainable depth in plain networks; activation-matched initialization comparisons; orthogonal versus Gaussian tanh initialization; and 10,000-layer plain convolutional networks.

record.verdict_notes: The record supplies no rows to correct. Figure 4's omitted numerical values and qualitative comparison are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as newly missing results. Exact per-depth values and Fixup-specific outcomes cannot be recovered from the supplied text. This study is not an original source for any listed version.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training classification error, corrupted or random labels, and effects of model size or training duration on training error.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, and varying student width relative to teacher width.

The paper's figure concerns residual networks without batch normalization and compares initializations; it does not test plain versus shortcut networks, training error, or the claim that shallower plain networks do better even with longer training.

It does not compare the cited activation-matched initializations on signal or gradient propagation across layers, nor test orthogonal versus Gaussian weights or 10,000-layer plain convolutional networks.
No above-stability-limit learning-rate experiment, loss-curvature trajectory, sharpness threshold, or divergence result is reported.

Figure 4 compares Fixup and other initializations on deep residual networks without batch normalization, but does not measure batch-normalization's accuracy-speed or learning-rate-tolerance effects, nor give numerical training-speed estimates.

relationships.condition: Deep CIFAR-10 ResNets using ZerO without batch normalization, evaluated after 15 epochs
relationships.reason: The Section 4 text accompanying Figure 4 says ZerO matches the batch-normalized baseline, extending the initialization-dependent qualification to batch normalization's accuracy-speed advantage. This verdict uses the text; no row ids exist. Initialization differs between these conditions, so this does not isolate batch normalization's causal effect.
relationships.display_finding: Unnormalized ZerO ResNets matched the batch-normalized baseline after 15 epochs, although the initialization difference prevents isolating normalization's effect.
